paras: The threatened lynching of Sampson Dey took place in Norfolk County, Virginia, in the late summer of 1888, after Dey, a Black tenant farmer, was arrested on suspicion of burning the barn of his landlord, George A. Wilson, at Green Ridge. Amid serious threats of lynching, the private detectives who had arrested him removed him to the Portsmouth jail, and he was bound over for trial.

Around 11 o'clock on the night of July 31, 1888, the large barn and outhouses on Wilson's Green Ridge farm in Butt's road District burned, together with corn, farming implements, wagons, mules and horses. A Norfolk correspondent put the loss at between $7,000 and $8,000, very nearly covered by insurance, and wrote that the buildings were "supposed to have been fired by an incendary." Wilson was described as one of the largest landholders in Norfolk County.

The J. W. Southward Detective Agency was hired and sent two operatives to Green Ridge, who arrested Dey, described as "colored" and a tenant on Wilson's plantation. Dey was examined before Justice Jordon (spelled Jordan in one printing) and sent on to the October term of the Norfolk County Court. According to a Portsmouth correspondent, "considerable excitement" followed in the community and "serious threats of lynching the prisoner were made." The detectives then spirited Dey away and "safely landed" him in the Portsmouth jail; who made the threats, and when, is not stated.
No report of Dey's trial at the October term, or of its result, was found in the coverage.

The episode reached print only in Richmond, where the same Portsmouth correspondence, dated September 20, ran in two papers the next day. The Daily Times headed it "Incendiary Fire in Norfolk County" with the subhead "Great Excitement—Threats of Lynching," while the Richmond Dispatch called it simply "An Incendiary Barn Burning" and left the threats out of its headline. Both printings praised the detectives' "prompt, diligent and earnest work," called the farm "the scene of the crime," and reported the lynching threats in a single sentence without comment. The Dispatch's earlier report of the fire itself named no suspect and said nothing of the later arrest.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Sampson Dey
bases: A Black man accused of arson was threatened with lynching after his arrest and was moved to the Portsmouth jail to prevent it; no attack is reported (A3, A4).

No one was killed: the papers report only 'serious threats of lynching the prisoner' in the community, which detectives forestalled by removing him to the Portsmouth jail (A3, A4); the episode is a threatened lynching, and who made the threats and how many is not stated.
The arrest and lynching threats come from one Portsmouth correspondence printed in two Richmond papers on the same day (A3, A4); A1 independently confirms only the barn fire itself.

accounts.label: Norfolk correspondent (fire)
accounts.gist: The barn and outhouses on Wilson's Green Ridge farm burned the night of July 31 with grain, implements, mules and horses, a loss of $7,000-$8,000; the fire was supposed to be incendiary.

accounts.label: Portsmouth special correspondence
accounts.gist: Southward detectives arrested Dey, a Black tenant, who was bound over to the October court; amid excitement and serious lynching threats, the detectives spirited him to the Portsmouth jail.

framing.detail: The Daily Times put 'Great Excitement—Threats of Lynching' in its headline and treated the threats as a matter of course, crediting the detectives' work and calling Dey 'the prisoner' while presenting the arson charge without qualification ('the scene of the crime').
The Richmond Dispatch ran the same text under the headline 'An Incendiary Barn Burning', leaving the lynching threats out of the headline.
